entries.6970ed063f204f90a00fd0368c16cfa6547099ca: <div sID="gen12456" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="108" osisID="Ps.108" sID="Ps.108"/> <div eID="gen12456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12457" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12458" type="x-p"/> This psalm begins with praise and concludes with prayer, and faith is at work in both. I. David here gives thanks to God for mercies to himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.108.1-Ps.108.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He prays to God for mercies for the land, pleading the promises of God and putting them in suit, <reference osisRef="Ps.108.6-Ps.108.13">ver. 6-13</reference>. The former part it taken out of <reference osisRef="Ps.57.7-Ps.57.11 Ps.108.1-Ps.108.5">Ps. lvii. 7</reference>, &c., the latter out of <reference osisRef="Ps.60.5-Ps.60.12 Ps.108.6-Ps.108.13">Ps. lx. 5</reference>, &c., and both with very little variation, to teach us that we may in prayer use the same words that we have formerly used, provided it be with new affections. It intimates likewise that it is not only allowable, but sometimes convenient, to gather some verses out of one psalm and some out of another, and to put them together, to be sung to the glory of God. In singing this psalm we must give glory to God and take comfort to ourselves.
entries.63b8da2d150b9e143e6814cc73555df45568a41d: <div eID="gen12458" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12457" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Directions for Praising God.</title> <div sID="gen12459" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O God, my heart is fixed; I will sing and give praise, even with my glory. <hi type="super">2</hi> Awake, psaltery and harp: I <hi type="italic">myself</hi> will awake early. <hi type="super">3</hi> I will praise thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , among the people: and I will sing praises unto thee among the nations. <hi type="super">4</hi> For thy mercy <hi type="italic">is</hi> great above the heavens: and thy truth <hi type="italic">reacheth</hi> unto the clouds. <hi type="super">5</hi> Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens: and thy glory above all the earth; <div eID="gen12459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12460" type="x-p"/> We may here learn how to praise God from the example of one who was master of the art. 1. We must praise God with fixedness of heart. Our heart must be employed in the duty (else we make nothing of it) and engaged to the duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.108.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">O God! my heart is fixed,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">I will sing and give praise.</hi> Wandering straggling thoughts must be gathered in, and kept close to the business; for they must be told that here is work enough for them all. 2. We must praise God with freeness of expression: I will praise him <hi type="italic">with my glory,</hi> that is, with my tongue. Our tongue is our glory, and never more so than when it is employed in praising God. When the <hi type="italic">heart is inditing</hi> this <hi type="italic">good matter</hi> our <hi type="italic">tongue</hi> must be as <hi type="italic">the pen of a ready writer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Ps. xlv. 1</reference>. David's skill in music was his glory, it made him famous, and this should be consecrated to the praise of God; and therefore it follows, <hi type="italic">Awake</hi> my <hi type="italic">psaltery and harp.</hi> Whatever gift we excel in we must praise God with. 3. We must praise God with fervency of affection, and must stir up ourselves to do it, that it may be done in a lively manner and not carelessly (<reference osisRef="Ps.108.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Awake, psaltery and harp;</hi> let it not be done with a dull and sleepy tune, but let the airs be all lively. <hi type="italic">I myself will awake early</hi> to do it, with all that is within me, and all little enough. Warm devotions honour God. 4. We must praise God publicly, as those that are not ashamed to own our obligations to him and our thankful sense of his favours, but desire that others also may be in like manner affected with the divine goodness (<reference osisRef="Ps.108.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will praise thee among the people</hi> of the Jews; nay, <hi type="italic">I will sing to thee among the nations</hi> of the earth. Whatever company we are in we must take all occasions to speak well of God; and we must not be shy of singing psalms, though our neighbours hear us, for it looks like being ashamed of our Master. 5. We must, in our praises, magnify the mercy and truth of God in a special manner (<reference osisRef="Ps.108.4">v. 4</reference>), mercy in promising, truth in performing. The heavens are vast, but the mercy of God is more capacious; the skies are high and bright, but the truth of God is more eminent, more illustrious. We cannot see further than the heavens and clouds; whatever we see of God's mercy and truth there is still more to be seen, more reserved to be seen, in the other world. 6. Since we find ourselves so, defective in glorifying God, we must beg of him to glorify himself, to do all, to dispose all, to his own glory, to get himself honour and make himself a name (<reference osisRef="Ps.108.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be thou exalted, O God! above the heavens,</hi> higher than the angels themselves can exalt thee with their praises, <hi type="italic">and</hi> let <hi type="italic">thy glory</hi> be spread over <hi type="italic">all the earth. Father, glorify thy own name. Thou hast glorified it; glorify it again.</hi> It is to be our first petition, <hi type="italic">Hallowed be thy name.</hi>
entries.73e469f0dfec4ab8ce12828301251941b4a038db: <div eID="gen12460" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Directions for Praising God.</title> <div sID="gen12461" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> That thy beloved may be delivered: save <hi type="italic">with</hi> thy right hand, and answer me. <hi type="super">7</hi> God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth. <hi type="super">8</hi> Gilead <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine; Manasseh <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine; Ephraim also <hi type="italic">is</hi> the strength of mine head; Judah <hi type="italic">is</hi> my lawgiver; <hi type="super">9</hi> Moab <hi type="italic">is</hi> my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe; over Philistia will I triumph. 10 Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom? <hi type="super">11</hi> <hi type="italic">Wilt</hi> not <hi type="italic">thou,</hi> O God, <hi type="italic">who</hi> hast cast us off? and wilt not thou, O God, go forth with our hosts? <hi type="super">12</hi> Give us help from trouble: for vain <hi type="italic">is</hi> the help of man. <hi type="super">13</hi> Through God we shall do valiantly: for he <hi type="italic">it is that</hi> shall tread down our enemies. <div eID="gen12461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12462" type="x-p"/> We may here learn how to pray as well as praise. 1. We must be public-spirited in prayer, and bear upon our hearts, at the throne of grace, the concerns of the church of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.108.6">v. 6</reference>. It is God's <hi type="italic">beloved,</hi> and therefore must be ours; and therefore we must pray for its deliverance, and reckon that we are answered if God grant what we ask for his church, though he delay to give us what we ask for ourselves. "<hi type="italic">Save</hi> thy church, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou <hi type="italic">answerest me;</hi> I have what I would have." <hi type="italic">Let the earth be filled with God's glory, and the prayers of David are ended</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.19-Ps.72.20">Ps. lxxii. 19, 20</reference>); he desires no more. 2. We must, in prayer, act faith upon the power and promise of God—upon his power (<hi type="italic">Save with thy right hand,</hi> which is mighty to save), and upon his promise: <hi type="italic">God has spoken in his holiness,</hi> in his holy word, to which he has sworn by his holiness, and therefore <hi type="italic">I will rejoice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.108.7">v. 7</reference>. What he has promised he will perform, for it is the word both of his truth and of his power. An active faith can rejoice in what God has said, though it be not yet done; for with him saying and doing are not two things, whatever they are with us. 3. We must, in prayer, take the comfort of what God has secured to us and settled upon us, though we are not yet put in possession of it. God had promised David to give him, (1.) The hearts of his subjects; and therefore he surveys the several parts of the country as his own already: "<hi type="italic">Shechem</hi> and <hi type="italic">Succoth, Gilead</hi> and <hi type="italic">Manasseh, Ephraim</hi> and <hi type="italic">Judah,</hi> are all my own," <reference osisRef="Ps.108.8">v. 8</reference>. With such assurance as this we may speak of the performance of what God has promised to the Son of David; he will, without fail, give him the heathen for his <hi type="italic">inheritance and the utmost parts of the earth for his possession,</hi> for so has he <hi type="italic">spoken in his holiness;</hi> nay, of all the particular persons that were given him he will <hi type="italic">lose none;</hi> he also, as David, shall have the hearts of his subjects, <reference osisRef="John.6.37">John vi. 37</reference>. And, (2.) The <hi type="italic">necks of his enemies.</hi> These are promised, and therefore David looks upon <hi type="italic">Moab,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Edom,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Philistia,</hi> as his own already (<reference osisRef="Ps.108.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Over Philistia will I triumph,</hi> which explains <reference osisRef="Ps.60.8">Ps. lx. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">Philistia, triumph thou because of me,</hi> which some think should be read, <hi type="italic">O my soul! triumph thou over Philistia.</hi> Thus the exalted Redeemer is set down at God's right hand, in a full assurance that all his enemies shall in due time <hi type="italic">be made his footstool, though all things are not yet put under him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.8">Heb. ii. 8</reference>. 4. We must take encouragement from the beginnings of mercy to pray and hope for the perfecting of it (<reference osisRef="Ps.108.10-Ps.108.11">v. 10, 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Who will bring me into the strong cities</hi> that are yet unconquered? Who will make me master of the country of <hi type="italic">Edom,</hi> which is yet unsubdued?" The question was probably to be debated in his privy council, or a council of war, what methods they should take to subdue the Edomites and to reduce that country; but he brings it into his prayers, and leaves it in God's hands: <hi type="italic">Wilt not thou, O God?</hi> Certainly thou wilt. It is probable that he spoke with the more assurance concerning the conquest of Edom because of the ancient oracle concerning Jacob and Esau, that <hi type="italic">the elder should serve the younger,</hi> and the blessing of Jacob, by which he was made Esau's lord, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.37">Gen. xxvii. 37</reference>. 5. We must not be discouraged in prayer, nor beaten off from our hold of God, though Providence has in some instances frowned upon us: "Though thou hast <hi type="italic">cast us off,</hi> yet thou wilt now <hi type="italic">go forth with our hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.108.11">v. 11</reference>. Thou wilt <hi type="italic">comfort us again</hi> after the time that thou <hi type="italic">hast afflicted us.</hi>" Adverse events are sometimes intended for the trial of the constancy of our faith and prayer, which we ought to persevere in whatever difficulties we meet with, and not to <hi type="italic">faint.</hi> 6. We must seek help from God, renouncing all confidence in the creature (<reference osisRef="Ps.108.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lord, give us help from trouble,</hi> prosper our designs, and defeat the designs of our enemies against us." It is not unseasonable to talk of trouble at the same time that we talk of triumphs, especially when it is to quicken prayer for help from heaven; and it is a good plea, <hi type="italic">Vain is the help of man.</hi> "It is really so, and therefore we are undone if thou do not help us; we apprehend it to be so, and therefore depend upon thee for help and have the more reason to expect it." 7. We must depend entirely upon the favour and grace of God, both for strength and success in our work and warfare, <reference osisRef="Ps.108.13">v. 13</reference>. (1.) We must do our part, but we can do nothing of ourselves; it is only <hi type="italic">through God that we shall do valiantly.</hi> Blessed Paul will own that even he can <hi type="italic">do nothing,</hi> nothing to purpose, <hi type="italic">but through Christ strengthening him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.13">Phil. iv. 13</reference>. (2.) When we have acquitted ourselves ever so well, yet we cannot speed by any merit or might of our own; it is God himself that <hi type="italic">treads down our enemies,</hi> else we with all our valour cannot do it. Whatever we do, whatever we gain, God must have all the glory.  <chapter eID="Ps.108"/> <div eID="gen12462" type="x-p"/>

entries.4f5a797d8801f3d055d42df70c4481ca082e3cb5: <chapter n="108" osisID="Ps.108" sID="Ps.108"/><div eID="gen10412" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6787"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 108</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.108.1-Ps.108.13">Psa 108:1-13</reference>. This Psalm is composed of <reference osisRef="Ps.108.1-Ps.108.5">Psa 108:1-5</reference> of <reference osisRef="Ps.57.7-Ps.57.11">Psa 57:7-11</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Ps.108.6-Ps.108.12">Psa 108:6-12</reference> of <reference osisRef="Ps.60.5-Ps.60.12">Psa 60:5-12</reference>. The varieties are verbal and trivial, except that in <reference osisRef="Ps.108.9">Psa 108:9</reference>, "over Philistia will I triumph," differs from <reference osisRef="Ps.60.8">Psa 60:8</reference>, the interpretation of which it confirms. Its altogether triumphant tone may intimate that it was prepared by David, omitting the plaintive portions of the other Psalms, as commemorative of God's favor in the victories of His people.</title> <div sID="gen10413" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.108"/>

entries.753eaaa1c72ab3f7cab4fe5ad937752bc55bc976: <div eID="gen22300" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22301" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22302" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22302" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22301" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22303" type="x-p"/> The psalmist encourages himself to praise the Lord for mercies he had received, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.1-Psa.108.5">Psa 108:1-5</reference>. He prays for the Divine succor, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.6">Psa 108:6</reference>; and encourages the people to expect their restoration, and the enjoyment of all their former privileges and possessions, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.7-Psa.108.13">Psa 108:7-13</reference>. <div eID="gen22303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22304" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is compounded of two Psalms which we have had already under review. The <reference osisRef="Psa.108.1">Psa 108:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.2">Psa 108:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.3">Psa 108:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.4">Psa 108:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.108.5">Psa 108:5</reference>, are the same with the <reference osisRef="Psa.57.7">Psa 57:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.57.8">Psa 57:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.57.9">Psa 57:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.57.10">Psa 57:10</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.57.11">Psa 57:11</reference> of <reference osisRef="Psa.57.1-Psa.57.11">Psa 57:1-11</reference> : And the <reference osisRef="Psa.108.6">Psa 108:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.7">Psa 108:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.8">Psa 108:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.9">Psa 108:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.10">Psa 108:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.11">Psa 108:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.108.12">Psa 108:12</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.108.13">Psa 108:13</reference>, are the same with the <reference osisRef="Psa.60.5">Psa 60:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.6">Psa 60:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.7">Psa 60:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.8">Psa 60:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.9">Psa 60:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.10">Psa 60:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.60.11">Psa 60:11</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.60.12">Psa 60:12</reference> of <reference osisRef="Psa.60.1-Psa.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference> : The variations are few, and of little moment, and the explanation may be seen in the notes on the preceding Psalms, which need not be repeated here. That the Pssalms referred to were made by David, and were applicable to the then state of his affairs, has been the opinion of many; and it is probable that the captives in Babylon composed this out of two above, and applied it to the state of their affairs. Their captivity being now ended, or nearly at an end they look and pray for their restoration to their own land, as amply as it was possessed in the most prosperous days of David. The Syriac considers it as a prophecy of the vocation of the Gentiles. The Hebrew and all the Versions attribute it to David. <div eID="gen22304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22305" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22306" type="x-p"/> Even with my glory - My greatest glory shall be in publishing thy praise. Some make the glory here to mean the Lord himself; some, the Ark of the covenant; some, the Soul of the psalmist; others, his Tongue; some, the Gift of Prophecy; and some, the psalmist's Spirit or Vein of poetry. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.57.8">Psa 57:8</reference>.
entries.85af11bc68b2773d79bfedf01963ddfed6e4cb7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22307" type="x-p"/> Among the people - The Jews. <div eID="gen22307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22308" type="x-p"/> Among the nations - The Gentiles. Wherever this Psalm is sung or read, either among Jews or Gentiles, David may be said to sing praise to God.
entries.dbb71b36c902602397e3ec093da75d0f6f2908ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22309" type="x-p"/> God hath spoken in his holiness - בקדשו bekodsho; some think this means in his Holy One, referring to the Prophet Jeremiah, who predicted the captivity, its duration of seventy years, and the deliverance from it.
entries.67fe351e828e8511cf37497710a857393b8ee203: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22310" type="x-p"/> The strong city - The possession of the metropolis is a sure proof of the subjugation of the country.
entries.e298a7254ad08beb310a94996b7bb84710f95c0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen22310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22311" type="x-p"/> Through God we shall do valiantly - From him we derive our courage, from him our strength, and by him our success. [For the Analysis, see the <reference osisRef="Psa.57.1-Psa.57.11">Psa 57:1-11</reference> (note) and <reference osisRef="Psa.60.1-Psa.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference> (note). Also see introduction to <reference osisRef="Psa.108.1-Psa.108.13">Psa 108:1-13</reference> (note)]  <chapter eID="Ps.108"/> <div eID="gen22311" type="x-p"/>

entries.d90812a8cdfcd01a903c858c7583e6c2baf8450c: <div eID="gen10046" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Two Elohimic Fragments Brought Together</title> <div sID="gen10047" type="x-p"/> The אודך in <reference osisRef="Ps.108.4">Psa 108:4</reference> and the whole contents of this Psalm is the echo to the הודוּ of the preceding Psalm. It is inscribed a <hi type="italic">Psalm-song by David</hi>, but only because it is compiled out of ancient Davidic materials. The fact of the absence of the למנצח makes it natural to suppose that it is of later origin. Two Davidic Psalm-pieces in the Elohimic style are here, with trifling variations, just put together, not soldered together, and taken out of their original historical connection. <div eID="gen10047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10048" type="x-p"/> That a poet like David would thus compile a third out of two of his own songs (Hengstenberg) is not conceivable.
entries.742bc6345bc6d0335ebb3a6bd2f50da0341cf1a0: <reference osisRef="Ps.108.1-Ps.108.5">Psa 108:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen10048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10049" type="x-p"/> This first half is taken from Ps. 57:8-12. The repetition of <hi type="italic">confident is my heart</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.57.1-Ps.57.11">Psa 57:1-11</reference> is here omitted; and in place of it the “my glory” of the exclamation, <hi type="italic">awake my glory</hi>, is taken up to “I will sing and will harp” as a more minute definition of the subject (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.5">Psa 3:5</reference>): He will do it, yea,his soul with all its godlike powers shall do it. <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.108.4">Psa 108:4</reference> is transformed out of the <hi type="italic">Adonaj</hi>; and <hi type="italic">Waw copul</hi>. is inserted both before <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.108.4">Psa 108:4</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.108.6">Psa 108:6</reference></hi>, contrary to <reference osisRef="Ps.57.1">Psa 57:1</reference>-11. מעל, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.108.5">Psa 108:5</reference> </hi>(as in <reference osisRef="Esth.3.1">Est 3:1</reference>), would be a pleasing change for עד if <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.108.5">Psa 108:5</reference></hi> followed <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.108.5">Psa 108:5</reference></hi> and the definition of magnitude did not retrograde instead of heightening. Moreover <reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Psa 36:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">Jer 51:9</reference> (cf. על in <reference osisRef="Ps.113.4">Psa 113:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.148.13">Psa 148:13</reference>) favour עד in opposition to מעל.
entries.22258bdfd6e2f5cbf09afc266e7bfc47ed966cc8: <reference osisRef="Ps.108.6-Ps.108.13">Psa 108:6-13</reference> <div eID="gen10049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10050" type="x-p"/> Ps. 60:7-14 forms this second half. The clause expressing the purpose with למען, as in its original, has the following הושׁיעה for its principal clause upon which it depends. Instead of ועננוּ, which one might have expected, the expression used here is וענני without any interchange of the mode of writing and of reading it; many printed copies have ועננו here also; Baer, following Norzi, correctly has וענני. Instead of ולי...לי, <reference osisRef="Ps.60.9">Psa 60:9</reference>, we here read לי...לי, which is less soaring. And instead of <hi type="italic">Cry aloud concerning me, O Philistia do I shout for joy</hi> (the triumphant cry of the victor); in accordance with which Hupfeld wishes to take התרועעי in the former as infinitive: “over (עלי instead of עלי) Philistia is my shouting for joy” (התרועעי instead of התרועעי, since the infinitive does not admit of this pausal form of the imperative). For עיר מצור we have here the more usual form of expression עיר מבצר. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.108.12">Psa 108:12</reference></hi> is weakened by the omission of the אתּה (הלא).  <chapter eID="Ps.108"/> <div eID="gen10050" type="x-p"/>

entries.2581e50b0c57928ea7546e0aa4539f7284ea45ad:
PSALM 108
Psalm 108:1-13
A Song or Psalm of David.
1. My heart is prepared, O God! my heart is prepared; I will sing and give praise, even with my glory. 2. Awake, psaltery and harp: I will arise at break of day. 3. I will praise thee, O Jehovah! among the people; and sing unto thee among the nations: 4. Because thy goodness is great above the heavens, and thy truth unto the clouds. 5. Be thou, O God! exalted above the heavens; and thy glory above all the earth: 6. That thy chosen may be set free, save me by thy right hand, and hear me. 7. God has spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and measure the valley of Succoth. 8. Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the strength of my head: Judah is my lawgiver.
“Ou, mon duc.” — Fr. marg. “Or, my leader.”
9. Moab is the pot of my washing; over Edom I will cast my shoe; over Philistina I will triumph. 10. Who will bring me into the fortified city? who will bring me even unto Edom? 11. Wilt not thou, O God! who hadst repulsed us? and wentest not out, O God! with our armies? 12. Lord us help out of our tribulations; because the help of man is vain. 13. Through God we will do valiantly, and he shall trample under foot our enemies.
 
Because this psalm is composed of parts taken from the fifty-seventh and sixtieth psalms, it would be superfluous to repeat, in this place, what we have already said by way of exposition in those psalms.
“The 108th psalm is altogether made up of extracts from the others; its first part being identical (with the exceptions of a few slight variations) with the third division of the 57th; its second, with the second division of the 60th. And both these borrowed parts are discriminated, both in the 57th and 60th psalms, from the rest of the context by the word Selah. This is a remarkable fact, and illustrates strongly one of the functions of the Diapsalma. These parts were, then, to a certain degree, regarded as distinct compositions, which occasionally were disjointed from their original context; the very change of sentiment and strain, which originated the word Diapsalma, sanctioning such an occasional practice.” — Jebb’s Literal Version of the Book of Psalms, with Dissertations, volume 2, page 109.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="108" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CVIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A Song, <ns0:hi>or</ns0:hi> Psalm of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm is almost word for word taken out of two forego<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Psalms, the first five verses out of <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 57. 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. and the rest out of <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 60. 5, &c. to which the Reader must resort for the explication of it. This only is observable that the Psalmist designing to take the body of this Psalm out of <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 60. doth industriously lay aside that mournful Preface <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1, 2, 3, 4. and borrows one more pleasant out of <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 57. The reason of which change is supposed to be this, that <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 60. was composed in the time of his danger and distress, and the latter after his de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liverance.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. O God, my heart <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 57. 7, 8, &c.</ns0:note> is fixed, I will sing and give praise even with my glory <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either, 1. with my heart or soul, which is fixed for that work, as he said in the former branch. Or rather, 2. with my tongue, which is called a mans <ns0:hi>glory, Psal.</ns0:hi> 16. 9. comp. with <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2. 26. So the first branch describes the fixedness of his heart, to which this adds the expressions of his mouth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. Awake psaltery and harp: I <ns0:hi>my self</ns0:hi> will a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wake early.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. I will praise thee, O LORD, among the people: and I will sing <ns0:hi>praises</ns0:hi> unto thee among the nations.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. For thy mercy <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> great above the heavens: and thy truth <ns0:hi>reacheth</ns0:hi> unto the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> skies.</ns0:note> clouds.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. Be thou exalted, O God, above the hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vens: and thy glory above all the earth;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 60. 5, &c.</ns0:note> That thy beloved may be delivered: save <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> thy right hand and answer me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. God hath spoken in his holiness, I will re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyce, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. Gilead <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> mine, Manasseh <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> mine, Ephraim also <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the strength of mine head, Judah <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my law-giver.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. Moab <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my wash-pot, over Edom will I cast out my shoe: over Philistia will I triumph.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This he repeats in this place, either because, though the enemies were defeated and subdued, yet there was some strong city or cities which were not yet taken; or in way of thankful commemoration of Gods goodness in answering his former requests, as if he had said, I remember this day to thy glory and my own comfort, my former straits and dan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gers, which made me cry out, <ns0:hi>Who will bring me,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. <ns0:hi>Wilt</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>thou,</ns0:hi> O God, <ns0:hi>who</ns0:hi> hast cast us off? and wilt not thou, O God, go forth with our hosts?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:498" />12. Give us help from trouble: for vain <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the help of man.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. Through God we shall do valiantly: for he <ns0:hi>it is that</ns0:hi> shall tread down our enemies.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
